What you covered

You met Ada Lovelace, history's first programmer (class 1); Marie Curie, the only person with two Nobel Prizes in different sciences (class 2); Hedy Lamarr, from movie star to co-inventor of wireless technology (class 3); Malala Yousafzai, the youngest Nobel laureate in history (class 4); Frida Kahlo, who turned pain into universal art (class 5); Rigoberta Menchú, whose testimony reached the whole world (class 6); and Wangari Maathai, who changed a country by planting trees (class 7).

A repeating pattern

If you paid attention, you'll notice an uncomfortable pattern in several of these stories: brilliant work that was ignored in its time (Lovelace, Lamarr), recognition that came decades late or after death (Curie paid with her life, Kahlo was reevaluated after she died), or enormous personal risk for defending a cause (Malala, Menchú, Maathai).

🔬 A connection to another school: if you took Oliver Academy's Introduction to Medicine course, you might remember Rosalind Franklin, whose "Photo 51" was key to discovering the structure of DNA — and who also received very little recognition at the time. The same pattern, in a different field.

Why telling these stories in full matters

It's not about taking credit away from anyone else — it's that the full story is more accurate, more interesting, and more useful than the incomplete version. When an important part of who did what is systematically lost, what's left isn't just unfair — it's incomplete as knowledge.

💡 If you enjoyed this course, "Human Development for Women" in this same school complements these stories with practical tools for your own life — not just historical role models to admire, but concrete resources to use.
